case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: G.V. v. Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: Reversing the Commonwealth Court, the court held that an indicated report of child abuse may be entered and maintained on the statewide ChildLine Registry on the CPSL's legislatively prescribed substantial-evidence standard, and that due process does not require clear and convincing evidence at an expunction hearing.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Pennsylvania rule on the burden and standard of proof supporting a substantiated (indicated) finding and its maintenance on the registry.
key_cases.quote: the proper standard of proof is the legislatively established substantial evidence standard

key_cases.case_name: A.Y. v. Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the Commonwealth Court and remanded, holding that while hearsay is admissible in a child-abuse expungement hearing, uncorroborated hearsay alone cannot satisfy the agency's burden and the accused is entitled to due process, including consideration of character evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Leading Pennsylvania authority on the quality of evidence required to substantiate abuse against a named perpetrator.
key_cases.quote: Although less process is due in an administrative proceeding than where criminal charges have been brought, an administrative adjudication of suspected child abuse is of the most serious nature.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and reinstating the trial court, the court held that the rebuttable presumption of 23 Pa.C.S. § 6381(d) identifying the caregiver as the abuser applies even where a child was in the care of multiple responsible adults.
key_cases.relevance: Central Pennsylvania authority on identifying the perpetrator for a substantiated finding when several adults had care of the child.
key_cases.quote: when a child is in the care of multiple parents or other persons responsible for care, those individuals are accountable for the care and protection of the child

key_cases.holding: The court reversed, holding the evidence insufficient to find the mother a perpetrator of child abuse by omission and that the § 6381(d) presumption does not apply absent evidence the caregiver knew or should have known of the abuse or risk and disregarded it.
key_cases.relevance: The limiting counterpart to In re L.Z.: the caregiver presumption cannot manufacture a substantiated finding by omission.
key_cases.quote: we hold there was insufficient evidence to support the juvenile court's finding that Mother was a perpetrator of child abuse under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6303(b.1)

key_cases.case_name: Support Center for Child Advocates v. Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of the child's guardian ad litem's petition to intervene in the alleged perpetrator's ChildLine expunction appeal, holding the GAL had no statutory right to intervene and no interest not already represented by the Department.
key_cases.relevance: Identifies who may participate when a substantiated finding is challenged administratively: the Department defends the report, not the child's own counsel.
key_cases.quote: H.M.'s G.A.L. has no right to intervene "conferred by statute," nor has he stated an interest such that his participation "is in the public interest."

key_cases.case_name: R. v. Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: Affirming the Commonwealth Court, the court held that an alleged perpetrator was not denied due process at a ChildLine expunction hearing where the hearing examiner who decided the case had not observed all the witnesses and the child testified in camera subject to cross-examination, because the CPSL narrowly limits who may learn of an indicated report.
key_cases.relevance: The Supreme Court's earlier construction of the process due when an indicated report resting on substantial evidence is challenged, and necessary background to G.V.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that R. received all the process he was due under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days in all cases; reasons for delay must be recorded if not completed within 30 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Investigation commenced by the county agency
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The particular reasons for delay past 30 days must be described in the child protective service record and made available to the department to determine whether the county agency strictly followed 23 Pa.C.S. Ch. 63 and whether it is subject to action under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6343

timeline_requirements.deadline: 90 days to request an administrative review by, or appeal and request a hearing before, the secretary to amend or expunge an indicated report; the department sends notice of the secretary's decision within 60 days of a request for administrative review
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Notice to a person named as perpetrator, or to a school employee named, of the status of the indicated report
